summary.text: Homo sapiens is a distinct species of the hominid family of primates, a family that includes all the great apes.
Over their evolutionary history, humans gradually developed traits such as bipedalism, dexterity and complex language.
Modern humans interbred with archaic humans, so human evolution was not a straight line but weblike.

items.prompt: Modern humans and archaic humans interbred. What does that imply about how to draw human ancestry?

options.label: As a straight ladder where each species replaces the last
As separate branches that never touch each other
As a web of connections, not a straight line
As a closed circle that returns to its starting point

items.explain: Because modern humans interbred with archaic humans, their evolution was not linear but weblike.

items.prompt: Molecular evidence compares the great apes closest to humans. In what order did they break away from the line leading to humans?

options.label: Gorillas first, then chimpanzees
Chimpanzees first, then gorillas
Both groups at exactly the same moment
Neither group ever shared a line with humans

items.explain: Molecular evidence suggests that between 8 and 4 million years ago, first the gorillas, and then the chimpanzees, split off from the line leading to the humans.

items.prompt: A fossil hunter searches wet tropical forest floors for ancient ape bones and finds very few. What probably explains it?

options.label: Apes never lived in forests during that period
Fossils can only form in dry caves
These apes evolved too recently to leave any fossils
Acidic rain forest soils dissolve bone, so little is preserved

items.explain: The fossil record of gorillas and chimpanzees is limited partly because rain forest soils tend to be acidic and dissolve bone, along with sampling bias.

items.prompt: Which is older in the fossil record: the first members of the genus Homo, or anatomically modern humans?

options.label: The genus Homo, which appears over 2 million years ago
Modern humans, who appear before any Homo species
Both appear at the same time
Modern humans, who predate the australopiths

items.explain: The Homo genus is evidenced by H. habilis over 2 million years ago, while anatomically modern humans emerged in Africa approximately 300,000 years ago.

items.prompt: Some researchers argue that humans may not come from a chimpanzee-like ancestor. What do they suggest about chimpanzees?

options.label: They are unchanged copies of the shared ancestor
Their form and behaviour may have evolved after the split
They evolved their traits before the split
They never shared an ancestor with humans

items.explain: These authors suggest the behaviour and morphology of chimpanzees may have evolved subsequent to the split from the ancestor they share with humans.

items.prompt: Experts debate whether the 'robust' australopiths belong in the same genus as the 'gracile' ones. If they form a genus of their own, what follows?

options.label: They would be renamed Homo
They would be merged into Ardipithecus
They may be given their own name, Paranthropus
They would lose their species names

items.explain: If these species constitute their own genus, they may be given their own name, Paranthropus.

paragraphs.heading: Our place among the apes
paragraphs.text: Humans, Homo sapiens, are one species within the hominid family of primates, the family that holds all the great apes. Over a long history, our ancestors slowly gained traits such as bipedalism, dexterity and complex language. Studying where humans came from draws on several sciences, including anthropology, paleontology and genetics.

paragraphs.heading: From early primates to apes
paragraphs.text: Primates split from other mammals about 85 million years ago, and their earliest fossils are more than 55 million years old. Much about their beginnings is still unknown, because so few fossils survive. Over time primates branched into a series of groups, one of which led to the apes. The apes in turn gave rise to the hominids and the gibbons, which went their separate ways some 15–20 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Splitting from our cousins
paragraphs.text: The African hominids parted from the orangutans about 14 million years ago. Molecular clues point to the gorillas and then the chimpanzees branching off, at some point from 8 to 4 million years ago, from the line that led to humans. Human DNA is about 98.4% identical to chimpanzee DNA when single nucleotide polymorphisms are compared. Yet fossils of gorillas and chimpanzees are scarce, probably in part because acidic rainforest soils dissolve bone, and in part because of sampling bias.

paragraphs.heading: The earliest possible ancestors
paragraphs.text: Some researchers place the oldest fossils on the human line at Sahelanthropus tchadensis, about 7 million years ago, and Orrorin tugenensis, about 6 million. After them came Ardipithecus, between 5.5 and 4.4 million years ago. Ardipithecus ramidus shares some features with bonobos, such as smaller differences between males and females.

paragraphs.heading: Not descended from chimps
paragraphs.text: Some researchers argue that many basic human adaptations arose in the ancient forests and woodlands of Africa. If so, humans may not have evolved from a chimpanzee-like ancestor, as was long assumed. Instead, chimpanzees may have developed much of their behaviour and body shape after they split from the ancestor they share with us.

paragraphs.heading: Australopithecus and Homo
paragraphs.text: The genus Australopithecus appeared in eastern Africa around 4 million years ago, spread across the continent, and died out around 2 million years ago. Several kinds lived during that span, including the species anamensis, afarensis, sediba and africanus. Our own genus, Homo, shows up with Homo habilis more than 2 million years ago. Anatomically modern humans emerged in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago.

paragraphs.heading: A web, not a ladder
paragraphs.text: Human evolution did not run along a single straight line. Modern humans interbred with archaic humans, so the pattern of our ancestry looks more like a web. Even within one period, scholars still debate how to group some species: the species robustus and boisei may belong with the australopiths or may form a genus of their own, Paranthropus.
